Alright, so here we have an anomaly that is literally a rip in time allowing creatures from ye olde past to be born in the present. The neat effect aside, you'd think the SCP Foundation's Temporal Anomalies department would be all over it. As such, a potential link could work as follows:

Recommend editing this:

The products of SCP-561 may only be moved by authorized personnel to whatever site is necessary for testing. Any products of SCP-561 found outside the fenced perimeter may be terminated on sight unless they are accompanied by appropriate personnel, or are part of Group N (see Addendum 561-1).

To this:

The products of SCP-561 may only be moved by authorized personnel to whatever site is necessary for testing. Any products of SCP-561 found outside the fenced perimeter may be terminated on sight unless they are accompanied by appropriate personnel, or are part of Group N (see Addendum 561-1).

I suggest this as an inline link for two reasons. First, I feel adding a new addendum for just the sake of this link would break the articles flow a little. Second, the Temporal Anomalies Department are technically the authorized personnel for a temporal anomaly.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

I second the request to add more scientific terminology and genus names to the species - along with removing the ancient rhino expungement. "Running bears with wolf-like limbs" - without mentioning they appear to be giant short-faced bears? On that note, I'm still not sure whether the time period is supposed to be the Pliocene Epoch (older) or the Pleistocene Epoch (more recent) - Pleistocene seems most likely from the wildlife referenced.

The thing that made me twitch was the reference to hoping some cetacean would pop out a Basilosaurus…not even remotely Pliocene (much less Pleistocene). They were around about 30-40 million years prior.

LOVE the idea, but some parts went too much against my sciency knowlodge and bucked against suspension of disbelief…so, no-voted. Would up vote in a heartbeat if the tone sounded more legit/scientific.

item.title: Re: Rhinoceros
item.content:encoded:
What about the Indricotherium? The biggest mammal walking on Earth. And the Brontotherium, Arsinoitherium and Uintatherium?
On a side note: I love this article, but the lack of scientific and techincal nouns made my animal-lover soul cringe a little. "Deers the size of a moose" = NOT TECHICALLY GOOD; "deers apparently of the genus Megaceros" = good. "primitive equines, some relatively small in size and labeled "cripplingly adorable" by staff members." = yuck; " primitive equines, primarily from the Eohippus and Hipparion genera" = way better. And so on and so forth. I'd suggest to the author to add more scientific nouns and techical terms, without forgetting to delete the rhinoceros' expungement - which, I feel, is pretty useless.
Upvoted, but please, someone do something for those nouns.
P.S.: Ancient elephants didn't only consist of mammoths and mastodons. Why do everyone never think of the Gonfotherium or the Platybelodon? Never mind, I forgot of the "morphologic-resemblance" thing. They aren't very similar to actual elephants…

This is a very minor, very technical complaint, but to a statistician, "current results suggest that affected offspring may be assigned to Pliocene-era species, not novel species, with a confidence interval of 99%" does not make sense. Unless this is the customary usage in a relevant field, I think you might want to say "with 99% confidence" — or bring up p-values if you want to get technical! (Confidence intervals are for values, not test results.)

Overall I loved it.
